summary:
Consensual same-sex intimacy was criminalised in Mongolia's Criminal Code of 1961 and decriminalised in 1993, when all references were removed. The age of consent is 16 regardless of sexual orientation.

Protection against discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity is spread across several instruments rather than a single equality statute. Section 14.1.1 of the Penal Code, in force since 1 July 2017, prohibits discrimination on both grounds. Article 6 of the Labour Code, in force since 2022, prohibits discrimination based on sexual orientation, gender identity and gender expression. Article 1.3.2 of the revised Criminal Law adopted on 3 December 2015 bars discrimination in criminalisation and sentencing on grounds including sexual and gender orientation. No comprehensive equality law is in place.

Hate-crime and hate-speech provisions cover gender identity. The Criminal Code adopted on 3 December 2015 named gender identity and sexual orientation as protected grounds for hate crimes; the code was scheduled to take effect on 1 September 2016 and was postponed to 1 July 2017. Section 10(1)(2)(14) of the Penal Code aggravates penalties for homicides motivated by hate towards the victim's gender identity or sexual orientation, and hate speech on the basis of gender identity is outlawed.

Article 16(11) of the Constitution defines marriage as based on the equality and mutual consent of a man and a woman who have reached the age determined by law, with State protection for family, motherhood and child. Same-sex relationships are not recognised, and same-sex couple households are ineligible for the protections available to opposite-sex couples. No union recognition of any kind is available. LGBT groups can register.

A June 2009 amendment to Article 20(1) of the Civil Registration Law allows transgender people to change their legal gender on birth certificates or citizen identification cards following sex reassignment surgery.

Enforcement of the hate-crime provisions remains weak. As of August 2018 the LGBT Centre had trained more than 300 police officers, prosecutors and judges on handling hate crimes, and reporting from October 2019 puts the figure at over 500 trained after an officer assaulted a detained transgender woman. The police force now has guidelines requiring officers to address transgender detainees by their identified gender regardless of identity documents. Despite this training, local reports and activists say police continue to disregard or not take seriously complaints of hate crimes against LGBT people, and attacks often result in no punishment.

Documented violence against transgender people includes a September 2009 incident in which a hyper-nationalist group kidnapped three transgender women in broad daylight at a promenade in Ulaanbaatar, drove them to a cemetery on the city outskirts, and beat, sexually assaulted and forced them to perform sexual acts on the perpetrators as a warning. The attack was not reported to police. Other documented attacks include the 2001 rape, abduction and stabbing of a lesbian woman by two men and a February 2014 sexual assault on a gay man by a neo-Nazi group; such violence is often not reported to police for fear of victimisation and reprisal. The most recent documented attack in this record is from February 2014; no later incident is recorded.

Survey data on the climate facing LGBT people in Mongolia is dated. A 2012 National Human Rights Commission survey of LGBT people found that almost 80% had experienced broadly categorised 'human-rights abuse' during the preceding three years, and almost three-quarters had considered suicide because of intolerance; the survey window closed in 2012. A 2019 report found 79% of LGBT-identified young people had experienced bullying, discrimination or ostracism. A 2013 report found over 73% of LGBT Mongolians had considered suicide due to social non-acceptance and intolerance. Mongolian culture is and has remained strongly heteronormative, and ostracism, harassment and violence persist socially and systemically despite the 2017 protections.

In June 2014 the law provided no additional penalty for bias-motivated violence and no requirement for law enforcement to record a suspected bias motive. A January 2014 working-group draft that would have added hate-bias motive as an aggravating factor, with penalties, reparations and police training, was replaced in late May 2014 by generalised discrimination references. In May 2014 the Government announced it would consider anti-discrimination legislation following public outcry.

Sexual orientation and gender identity are discussed in the sex education curriculum introduced in 1998, though teachers may choose whether to cover these topics.
tangentialFactors:
The 2018 Pride event and the advocacy of the LGBT Centre in Ulaanbaatar mark visible organising, but the wider scene has virtually no presence, venues or activism. A 2008 account describes two organisations holding furtive monthly parties where attendees fear being outed.

A December 2018 social experiment in Ulaanbaatar placed three LGBT people, a gay man, a lesbian and a transgender man, roadside to observe reactions; online responses ranged from death threats to negative comments to positive ones, and the experiment showed the public were more welcoming of the lesbian and the trans man than of the gay man.

The 2012 National Human Rights Commission survey covered LGBT people broadly rather than transgender people specifically, and its window closed in 2012; the 2019 bullying figure covers LGBT-identified young people as a group. Neither is a current trans-specific prevalence measure.

outOfScopeNotes:
The ADB legal-status review holds no source finding for Mongolia.

Whether the 2014 announcement that the Government would consider anti-discrimination legislation produced any enacted comprehensive equality statute is unresolved in this inventory; the sources describe protections as fragmented with no comprehensive law.

The current status of the police guidelines requiring officers to address transgender detainees by their identified gender, first reported in October 2019, is not sourced beyond that date.

No current trans-specific violence rate with a denominator is available; the documented incidents are individual cases from 2001, 2009 and 2014, and no later incident is recorded.
